description: Factor 1 is composed of 12 articles, most of them experimental research. Inappropriate consumption behaviors are related to alcohol, unbalanced eating, and aggressive social behaviors. The main article of this factor is by Sheehan and Lau-Barraco (2016), in which the authors review the literature on aggressive behavior derived from alcohol consumption, proposing a model that helps to explain these relationships. This topic derives from Factor 1 and is presented in the previous bibliographic coupling period, which mainly addresses ego depletion related to food and aggressive behavior.

Factor 2 consists of five articles, all experimental designs. This topic presents relations with ED that we did not observe in previous analyses, such as religiosity, advertising, pro-environmental consumption, and financial education. The central article of this factor is by Achtziger et al. (2016), in which the authors address the effects of ED on decision making, considering automatic processes. This factor is the most plural among the identified topics and demonstrates the scope of research on ED in human behavior. The statement that the factor presents a new research topic was only made possible by comparing the two periods of the same analysis in sequence.

Factor 3 consists of four articles, all experimental research addressing ED and its effects on organizational behavior. The articles address social exclusion, abusive supervision, organizational citizenship based on air pollution, and inconsistency of values between employees and organizations, all related to ED in the organizational environment. The article by Deng et al. (2016) is central to this factor and addresses the incongruous value between employee and organization as a negative work condition. The previous research analysis did not introduce this topic. Therefore, it is considered a new topic in studies of ED.

Factor 4 consists of four articles, including theoretical and experimental research. This factor derives from the evolution of Factor 3 presented in the previous bibliographic coupling period, which addresses decision making in consumption and, consequently, impulsive buying. We also observed this topic in the co-citation analysis of this research, which indicates that it is a mature topic in research on ED in CB. The central article of this factor is by Moayery et al. Factors 5 and 6 are composed of three articles each, being theoretical and experimental research. The factors are not focused on a single topic, given the low number of articles that compose them. Therefore, they are factors with plural perspectives. Nonetheless, the factors present new elements in research on ED in CB. Two articles on these factors address the regulatory focus on consumption, with the relationship affected by self-regulation. Others address retail buying behavior and luxury consumption related to self-regulation. The elements of these factors were not observed in the previous analysis of the present study, and they demonstrate the scope of research on ED in CB.

Factor 7 consists of three articles, one theoretical and two empirical. As observed in other factors, although factors with few articles or references do not form a focused topic, they present interesting results for discussion. The theoretical article by Baumeister and Vohs (2016) is central to this factor. This article was published as a book chapter, and the authors argued that the limited resource strength model is the best explanation for ED. This research goes against the theoretical arguments made by Inzlicht and Schmeichel (2012) in their article, highlighted in Factor 2 of the previous bibliographic coupling period. That article proposes the processing model to explain ED through underlying mechanisms of motivation and attention. With the analysis of the last decade, divided into two periods, it is possible to observe the evolution of some topics from the first to the second period and which were the new topics that emerged in recent research on ED in CB. The analysis of the evolution of the two periods begins with Factor 1 of the two periods, relating to inadequate food consumption caused by failed self-regulation. Factor 2 of the first period is also related to Factor 1 of the second period due to the influence of glucose on ED, reflecting inappropriate behaviors. Factor 3 of the first period is related to Factor 4 of the second period. The evolution of research in decision making presents studies on the failures in self-regulation that lead to impulsive purchases, affecting long-term objectives.
